# University College London (UCL) – Summary
University College London (UCL) is a major public research university located in Bloomsbury, Central London, founded in 1826 as a secular alternative to Oxford and Cambridge. It became University College, London in 1836 and gained full independence as University College London in 1976. UCL is a member of the University of London, the Russell Group, and several international research alliances, including forming the Science and Engineering South alliance and being a founding partner of the Alan Turing Institute and the Francis Crick Institute. UCL is widely recognized for leading the field in research, with significant contributions in disciplines such as medicine, engineering, neuroscience, and the humanities. In the 2021 Research Excellence Framework, UCL ranked second in the UK for research power, and it consistently places among the top global universities in all major international rankings (8th in 2023 QS World University Rankings).
UCL has a diverse and highly international student body, with over 46,000 students—more than half from outside the UK—and notable representation from China and around the world. It has eleven faculties spanning a broad spectrum of disciplines, with substantial resources in libraries, museums, and research centers. UCL operates a substantial main campus in Bloomsbury and a new campus at UCL East in Stratford, with extensive student accommodation and sustainability initiatives. The university is committed to widening access and supports students from disadvantaged backgrounds with contextual offers and foundation programs. UCL alumni and staff include 33 Nobel laureates and several notable figures such as Francis Crick, Charles Kao, and Joseph Lister. Student life is vibrant, with over 250 clubs and societies, a strong tradition of student activism, and inter-university rivalry, especially with King's College London.
